title: Dark Factory: OpenClaw Ships Faster Than You Can Read the Diff — Vincent Koc, OpenClaw

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary object is using autonomous coding agents (Codex) to write, refactor, and ship software at massive scale across parallel swim lanes and PR workflows. OpenClaw is a software project driven by coding agents, and the dot-skills agent development environment and Geppetto tooling touch the developer-platforms domain. Content spans active development at extreme commit velocity, productionization of a plugin architecture overnight, and scaling to 60-70 concurrent agents and 60k open PRs. Assumes working knowledge of Git work trees, CI/CD pipelines, autonomous coding agents, and parallel session management; not introductory material. Recorded conference presentation by Vincent Koc on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. All cited evidence anchors are direct transcript excerpts graded as 'said_in_transcript'.

summary:
Vincent Koc introduces himself as a core OpenClaw maintainer with a day job, presenting on what he calls 'dark factories' and how OpenClaw ships faster than you can read the diff. He opens with a personal anecdote about using early VR goggles for three hours and vomiting afterward, drawing an analogy to working at the bleeding edge: it is janky and uncharted, much like running AI agents at massive commit velocity. He draws a parallel to Britain's Industrial Revolution, arguing that software engineering is undergoing its own productionization moment where engineers become factory managers and the bottleneck shifts from hands-on coding to taste and judgment.

He cites examples of autonomous agent adoption: Anthropic building a C compiler, Spotify reportedly no longer writing code by hand, Steve Yegge pushing ~50 PRs daily as a 'vibe maintainer,' and OpenClaw peaking at 800 commits per day across 10-15 maintainers who all have day jobs. Vincent personally hit close to 3,000 commits on March 15th, with his commit history literally showing when he sleeps. He distinguishes 'commit maxing' from a more opinionated 'bot looping' approach that needs smarter reward mechanisms.

The centerpiece is the 'great refactor.' While at Nvidia helping build NemoClaw, he and Peter ran approximately 60-70 agents including sub-agents, with about 15 swim lanes visible in the foreground. A maintainer's folder reorganization catalyzed a decision to rip the codebase into a plugin architecture. The result: 2,700 commits, close to a million lines changed, 82% of the core codebase touched in one night, with plugins launched by morning. When tests failed at 1 AM, Vincent feared he had 'vibed too hard,' but AI-generated unit tests that had overfit to the original code served as an unintended safety net.

Vincent explains his swim lane method: 5-20 parallel coding sessions organized by type (CI, features, bugs, P0/P1 triage, release monitoring). Some lanes need no babysitting; others require active conversation. He adopted Git work trees to isolate PRs but ended up with 70-80 active work trees daily, which hammered his machine, forcing custom self-healing logic into his Codex session. An alternative approach Peter uses is simply cloning the repo 10 times and pointing separate Codex sessions at each clone.

Vincent describes 'reading the reasoning tokens' — a Matrix-like intuition developed through sheer volume of token maxing. He can sense when an agent's explanation sounds off: it is waffling, not making sense, or does not seem to know what it is doing. This mirrors managing people: if someone starts bullshitting, you intervene. He may nuke the session or leave the code for another maintainer and return days later. He frames managing 10+ agents as analogous to managing 10+ staff, drawing on his experience leading 30-40 person teams in airlines and other large organizations. The soft skills — knowing how to ask agents what is going on and detecting when they are bullshitting — are what matter.

He details the agent development environment: 'dot skills' (analogous to dot files), open-sourced on GitHub, including skills for technical documentation co-created with developer experience engineers. He uses a skills gem called Geppetto (to which he contributes) and deploys via vercel.skills.sh. PR management is itself engineered: OpenClaw faces approximately 60,000 open PRs, prompting multiple maintainers to attempt solutions. Vincent's approach uses semantic graphing and vector embeddings across GitHub data, with one PR containing 73,106 edges. The team deduplicates issues and uses pressure signals — when enough contributors flag the same problem, it warrants attention. Surprisingly, the project also runs evals: a fake Slack environment with both synthetic and real models tests that each provider and channel works after refactoring. He closes with the thesis: 2025 was about token maxing; 2026 is about not wasting them — token efficiency and agent-in-the-loop.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Engineers are transitioning from hands-on coders to factory managers; the new bottleneck is taste, judgment, and brain space — not typing speed or token supply.

The 'great refactor' produced 2,700 commits, ~1 million lines changed, and touched 82% of the core codebase overnight, shipping a plugin architecture by morning using 60-70 agents across ~15 swim lanes.

sections.title: Introduction and Personal Background
sections.summary: Vincent introduces himself as a core OpenClaw maintainer with a day job. He shares a 2013 VR goggles anecdote where he played Team Fortress 2 for three hours and vomited afterward, using it as an analogy for working at the bleeding edge: it is janky, horrific, and uncharted. He notes that shipping at OpenClaw's velocity gets him rate-limited by GitHub hourly.

sections.title: The New Industrial Revolution in Software
sections.summary: Vincent draws a parallel between Britain's Industrial Revolution and the current moment in software. Craftsmen and handlooms gave way to centralized mills; similarly, engineers writing code in editors are giving way to swarms across repos. Engineers are becoming factory managers and the bottleneck is now taste, not the weaver's hands. He notes the tension between his structured Evals day job and his blind-faith approach on OpenClaw.

sections.title: Autonomous Agent Adoption and Commit Velocity
sections.summary: Vincent cites organizations secretly and openly adopting autonomous agents: Anthropic building a C compiler, Spotify reportedly no longer hand-writing code, Steve Yegge pushing ~50 PRs daily as a 'vibe maintainer.' OpenClaw peaked at 800 commits/day across 10-15 maintainers. Vincent personally hit ~3,000 commits on March 15th, with his commit history revealing his sleep schedule. He distinguishes 'commit maxing' from a more opinionated 'bot looping' approach.

sections.title: Nvidia, NemoClaw, and the Great Refactor Catalyst
sections.summary: Vincent describes being at Nvidia with Peter building NemoClaw. Peter ran ~15 code sessions VPN'd into a Mac Studio; Vincent ran another 10-15. Together they had 60-70 agents including sub-agents, with ~15 foreground swim lanes. A maintainer's folder reorganization moved all MS Teams and Slack channel code, catalyzing a decision to refactor the entire codebase into a plugin architecture at 2 AM.

sections.title: The Great Refactor: Execution and Rescue
sections.summary: The refactor produced 2,700 commits, ~1 million lines changed, and touched 82% of the core codebase, with plugins launched by morning. At 1 AM tests were failing and Vincent feared he had 'vibed too hard.' The saving grace was AI-generated unit tests that had overfit to the original code: when they went green after ripping everything out, the team knew they were close to correct.

sections.title: Swim Lanes: The Factory Manager's Approach
sections.summary: Vincent explains his swim lane method: 5-20 parallel coding sessions organized by type. Lanes might include CI work, feature development, bug fixes, Docker or messaging channel issues, and P0/P1 triage using GitHub or Discord agent data. Some lanes need no babysitting; others require active conversation. He emphasizes that tokens are no longer the bottleneck; raw compute and brain space to monitor sessions are.

sections.title: Harness, Git Work Trees, and Compute Challenges
sections.summary: Vincent describes adopting Git work trees for PR isolation, which resulted in 70-80 active work trees daily and hammered his machine under heavy test harnesses. He built custom self-healing logic into his Codex session so it is aware of Git work trees and can recover when he hits the escape key, acknowledging the operational complexity this introduces.

sections.title: Reading Reasoning Tokens and Nuking Sessions
sections.summary: Vincent describes a Matrix-like intuition for monitoring agents: 'reading the reasoning tokens.' He can sense when an agent's explanation sounds off — it is waffling, not making sense, or does not seem to know what it is doing. This mirrors managing people: if someone starts bullshitting, you intervene. He may nuke the session, defer the code to another maintainer, or return days later. This intuition comes from sheer volume of token maxing over the prior year. He also notes Peter's simpler alternative: clone the repo 10 times and point separate Codex sessions at each clone.

sections.title: Agent Development Environment and Dot Skills
sections.summary: Vincent describes his 'agent development environment' built around dot skills (analogous to dot files), open-sourced on GitHub. Skills include technical documentation co-created with developer experience engineers. He uses a skills gem called Geppetto (to which he contributes) and deploys via vercel.skills.sh, with a process for maintaining and improving skills based on Codex session logs.

sections.title: PR Management, Semantic Graphing, and Evals
sections.summary: Vincent explains PR management at scale. OpenClaw has approximately 60,000 open PRs (corrected by an audience member). Multiple maintainers independently attempt clustering solutions, creating noise. Vincent's approach uses semantic graphing and vector embeddings across GitHub data — one PR had 73,106 edges. The team deduplicates issues and uses aggregate pressure as a signal to prioritize. He also reveals the project runs evals: a fake Slack with synthetic and real models to verify providers and channels work after refactoring.

sections.title: Managing Agents Like Staff and the 2026 Thesis
sections.summary: Vincent addresses the question of managing 10+ agents by comparing it to managing 10+ staff, drawing on his experience leading 30-40 person teams in airlines. For engineers, the soft skills matter: asking agents what is going on, detecting bullshit, and running the factory. He closes: 2025 was about token maxing; 2026 is about not wasting them — token efficiency and agent-in-the-loop.
